Pa. House passes bipartisan legislation to regulate artificial intelligence usage in healthcare
Rep. Greg Scott
September 30, 2026 | 3:49 PM
HARRISBURG, Sept. 30 –
The Pennsylvania House today passed bipartisan legislation that would regulate the application of artificial intelligence in healthcare, ensuring that all Pennsylvanians can have confidence that AI is being utilized in a beneficial manner when receiving clinical care or when insurers are reviewing coverage of specific healthcare recommendations, announced the legislation's co-prime sponsors, state Reps. Arvind Venkat, Joe Hogan, Tarik Khan, Bridget Kosierowski and Greg Scott.
House Bill 1925
would provide new regulations for how AI is utilized and reported by insurers, hospitals and clinicians. These groups would need to provide transparency to patients and the public as to how AI is being used in their companies or practice settings.
"The usage of AI is expanding rapidly into nearly every field, and healthcare is no exception," said
Venkat, D-Allegheny
. "As the General Assembly's only physician, I have seen this development take place in real time. It is vital that patients are confident that AI is being used responsibly and effectively in their care. I thank my House colleagues who partnered on this legislation and helped it to pass in a bipartisan manner. Protecting trust in our healthcare system is vital to the safety and future of all Pennsylvanians."
"Patients deserve to know when artificial intelligence is involved in their healthcare, and they should have full confidence that a qualified healthcare professional, not AI or an algorithm, remains responsible and accountable for their care," said
Khan, D-Phila
. "Our bill protects patients by establishing commonsense safeguards and increasing transparency and accountability as AI becomes a bigger part of healthcare."
"AI technology has the potential to make some healthcare processes more streamlined and efficient, but it's important that we stay ahead of its use as it adapts and changes," said
Scott, D-Montgomery
. "Patients deserve full transparency and confidence in their care. These guardrails ensure that when AI is used in the healthcare setting, it's being used responsibly and alongside expert, human care, too."
The legislation would also prevent clinicians from being superseded in their judgment by AI recommendations by requiring human decision-makers to make final decisions for a patient's care based on an individualized assessment if AI is used by insurers, hospitals or clinicians.
"As AI continues to grow as a tool in our lives, steps must be taken to ensure it does not become over-relied on," said
Hogan, R-Bucks
. "I recognize that it can be a valuable tool in medicine, but we must ensure that all final decisions are made by a human doctor. House Bill 1925 puts that regulation in place, ensuring the best care for patients across the Commonwealth."
"As a nurse for 30 years, I believe we need to install guardrails to ensure AI is being used in the most effective way when it comes to making decisions about patients' healthcare," said
Kosierowski, D-Lackawanna
. "This necessary legislation will ensure that experienced healthcare providers oversee AI assessments and make the final decisions concerning a patient's health or healthcare coverage."
To ensure that current laws related to privacy, safety, and anti-discrimination are upheld, H.B. 1925 would also require attestation from insurers to the PA Department of Insurance or PA Department of Human Services and from hospitals and other healthcare facilities to the PA Department of Health on how their required internal governance and use of AI is in compliance with these laws.
House Bill 1925 passed the House by a vote of 144-59. The bill will now move to the state Senate for consideration.

Scott applauds $725K investment in Conshohocken Fire Department
Rep. Greg Scott
September 17, 2026 | 12:18 PM
NORRISTOWN, Sept. 17 –
State Rep. Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, today applauded $725,000 in state funds awarded to Conshohocken Borough on behalf of the Conshohocken Fire Department.
The grant funding will be used to replace the fire department’s aging air service truck with a larger 2027 model.
“This grant is a significant investment in the safety and resilience of our community. By funding the replacement of the fire department’s aging air service truck, we are helping ensure that our volunteer firefighters have the reliable equipment they need to respond effectively when our residents need them most,” said Council President Tina Sokolowski. “Our volunteer fire service is made up of dedicated individuals who give their time, expertise, and commitment to protecting our borough. Supporting them with modern apparatus and equipment is one of the most important investments we can make in public safety.
“I want to thank Rep. Scott, Sen. Vince Hughes, and our state partners for recognizing this need and securing this funding. As volunteer fire companies across Pennsylvania face increasing operational and financial challenges, this grant represents a critical investment in the future of emergency services in Conshohocken and the safety of everyone who lives, works, and visits here.”
“As a volunteer firefighter myself, I know how aging equipment can slow down the response to fire emergencies,” said Scott. “Maintaining and upgrading trucks, equipment, and safety gear is necessary for all fire departments to deliver their best, most efficient emergency assistance. I am proud to have played a part in getting this funding for our local department and appreciate their ongoing dedication to our community.”
“I’m proud to announce this substantial state investment in our Conshohocken Fire Department, alongside Rep. Scott,” said Hughes. “If we expect our emergency response teams to show up in the face of danger and uncertainty, we need to ensure they have the necessary tools and resources to help our neighbors. Both Rep. Scott and I remain committed to working with local leaders in Conshohocken to strengthen infrastructure and support services for every resident in the Borough.”
The grants come from
Local Share Account
funds, which are approved and distributed by the
Commonwealth Financing Authority
.

NORRISTOWN, Sept. 16 –
State Rep. Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, and the Norristown Municipal Waste Authority applaud the allocation of $942,211 in state funding to rehabilitate portions of the sewer system in the municipality of Norristown.
According to a statement from the authority, the grant will fund trenchless pipe lining, point repairs, pipe replacement, and manhole improvements.

HARRISBURG, Sept. 14 –
State Reps. Melissa Shusterman, D-Chester, and Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, are announcing the introduction of legislation to guard against the potential catastrophic risks of frontier artificial intelligence models.

around the world over the past week have detailed concerns shared by CEOs of major AI companies regarding the alarming potential risks posed by the largest and most advanced AI models. These risks include catastrophic failures of the worldwide internet, bioweapons development, threats to financial, utility and infrastructure systems, and more.
In the absence of action at the federal level, Shusterman and Scott said Pennsylvania needs to be proactive in mitigating catastrophic risks related to AI. Their legislation would establish appropriate measures to do so and would be based on language from laws already passed with bipartisan support in other states, including California, Illinois and New York.
These measures would include requirements for developing and adhering to AI safety frameworks; creating a mechanism for reporting critical safety incidents; protecting whistleblowers who report catastrophic risks; and requiring third parties to conduct independent audits for compliance.
“AI has the potential for technological advancements and benefits,” Shusterman said. “However, government must ensure frontier models are not causing catastrophic harm to society. This is my bare minimum expectation. Currently, AI has no federal regulatory standards. Every other industry has governmental safeguards for good reasons -- AI requires the same level, or more. The possibility of rogue AI agents is not acceptable to me, and I urge my fellow legislators of our Commonwealth, as well as officials at every level of government, to take these risks seriously and act quickly. Our citizens are counting on us.”
“Ensuring strong safeguards around advanced AI systems is essential to protecting the wellbeing of our communities and the stability of our critical infrastructure,” Scott said.
“By acting now, Pennsylvania can take a responsible, forward-looking approach that matches the urgency of this rapidly evolving technology and aligns with efforts already underway in other states.”
In their memo to colleagues, circulated in August, Shusterman and Scott announced their intentions to introduce this legislation. The bill itself is expected to be introduced in the next few days.

State Rep. Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, welcomed Norristown Area High School student Sara Brundidge to Wednesday’s commemorative voting session at Congress Hall in Philadelphia.

HARRISBURG, Sept. 8 –
State Rep. Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, today announced that his Pennsylvania Universal Health Care Act—a publicly funded healthcare plan for every Pennsylvanian—has been formally introduced in the PA House.
“Health and wellness are determining factors in quality of life, longevity, happiness, and family success,” said Scott. “With our current federal administration, we won’t see national universal healthcare anytime soon. This bill ensures the great people of Pennsylvania have access to high-quality health coverage without out-of-pocket costs.”
House Bill 2763 would establish the freestanding Universal Health Care Act and the Office of Health Care within the Pennsylvania Department of Health to create a single-payer health system in Pennsylvania. The act would be funded by a combination of employer and employee contributions and would be available to every commonwealth resident, as well as nonresidents working at least 20 hours per week in Pennsylvania.
“Rising premium costs are forcing many hardworking families to drop their health insurance coverage, putting not only their health at risk, but also their financial stability,” said Scott. “Without insurance coverage, one unexpected health event can bankrupt a family. It’s in our best interest to ensure every resident in our state has reliable health insurance coverage.”

HARRISBURG, July 24 –
State Rep. Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, today released the following statement about the uptick in race-based threats directed at elected officials and the unified response by Montgomery County officials.
“The racist and hateful voicemail left for my friend, Delaware County Sheriff Siddiq Kamara, was sickening. There is no place for racism, Islamophobia, or hatred in our politics or our communities, and I hope the person responsible is held fully accountable,” Scott said.
“This is personal for me.
“My family and I have lived through this kind of hate. I've received death threats, been called the N-word, and even received a voicemail from someone who said they wished one of my relatives had been raped. Those words don't just target elected officials—they target our families, our children, and our humanity.
“That's why I'm grateful my colleagues across Montgomery County came together—to speak with one voice. Together, every countywide elected official, state senator, and state representative from Montgomery County signed the statement below condemning the racism, threats, and intimidation that Sheriff Kamara endured and that too many Black elected officials experience far too often.
“We cannot wait until hate makes headlines to condemn it. We must call it out every single time. Silence only gives hate room to grow.
“Political disagreement is part of democracy. Racism, bigotry, and threats of violence are not.
“I'm proud to stand with my colleagues in saying, clearly and unequivocally: there is no place for hate here.”

Pa. House votes to classify veterinary sedative as a Schedule III drug
Rep. Greg Scott
June 30, 2026 | 3:18 PM
HARRISBURG, June 30 –
The Pennsylvania House today passed a bill that would classify a naloxone-resistant animal sedative, medetomidine, as a Schedule III drug.
According to the bill’s prime sponsors, state Reps. Greg Scott and Liz Hanbidge, both of Montgomery County, this is a strategic move to stop the use of medetomidine in street drugs.
“We’re seeing increased use of medetomidine in fentanyl and fentanyl-related overdoses,” said Scott. “This is hugely dangerous. Unlike other sedatives that made it to the street drug market, medetomidine doesn’t respond to naloxone – people who overdose on medetomidine-laced fentanyl have a significantly higher risk of dying because overdose-reversing medicines don’t work.”
Medetomidine is a non-opioid sedative used by veterinarians. It is not approved for use in people. But data now shows that up to 80 percent of fentanyl samples tested in Pennsylvania contain it, increasing the risk of overdose for people who illegally use fentanyl.
“The rapid spread of medetomidine in Pennsylvania's illicit drug supply presents a serious and growing threat to public safety. This dangerous veterinary sedative makes overdoses more difficult to treat, puts first responders at greater risk, and places additional strain on our emergency medical system. As legislators, we have a responsibility to respond before more lives are lost, and that is why Rep. Scott and I introduced this bill,” said Hanbidge.
Studies show that between 75% and 90% of people experiencing withdrawal from medetomidine require ICU-level medical care. Classifying medetomidine as a Schedule III drug would still allow veterinarians to legally use the medicine for treating animals, while making the penalties for possessing or selling it illegally more substantial.
“We’re losing too many Pennsylvanians to the opioid epidemic, and this change is a simple yet impactful means of controlling a substance that is making it harder to save lives. We saw it work with xylazine, and I believe it can work again with medetomidine,” said Scott. “I’m grateful to my peers in the House for supporting our goals and the health and safety of so many of our families.”
In 2024, Pennsylvania designated another sedative drug, xylazine, a Schedule III controlled substance. In response, the use of xylazine in street drugs declined. The representatives hope repeating this tactic with medetomidine will have the same impact.
“I am pleased that this legislation has passed the House and look forward to the Senate doing the same,” said Hanbidge. “By establishing stronger controls on medetomidine, we are taking an important step to save lives, support the brave first responders and healthcare professionals who confront this crisis every day, and better protect Pennsylvanians from an increasingly dangerous drug supply.”
This bill is a companion to
S.B. 866.
H.B. 2529
passed the House today by a vote of 198-4.

HARRISBURG, June 29 –
The state House today voted unanimously to update the Pennsylvania Child Labor Act to allow 14- and 15-year-old emergency service volunteers to engage in training and firefighting activities until 10 p.m. on any night of the year.
The bill’s prime sponsor, state Rep. Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, said that this change will help support the pipeline of trained volunteers needed to respond to community emergencies.
“By some estimates, Pennsylvania has one-tenth of the volunteer firefighters we had in the 1970s,” Scott said. “Many of our emergency response organizations are chronically understaffed and unable to respond efficiently to calls. It’s a bad situation, and without action, it’s only going to get worse.”
Under the state’s Child Labor Act, minors can engage in training or firefighting activities until 10 p.m. the night before a school day. Yet on weekends, holidays and over summer academic breaks, that curfew is only 9 p.m.
“The difference between school nights and non-school nights is an oversight that prevents engaged, ambitious young people from helping their communities after an arbitrary timepoint. Making their curfew 10 p.m. all year is a small change that can make a huge difference in an emergency,” Scott said.
Under state law, youth may join a volunteer fire company as young as age 14 with written consent from a parent or guardian.

now heads to the Senate for consideration.

HARRISBURG, June 23 –
State Rep. Greg Scott today announced the House Commerce Committee approved his bill that would allow more electric vehicle manufacturers to sell directly to consumers in Pennsylvania.
A 2014 amendment to the Board of Vehicles Act made it possible for EV manufacturers to sell directly to the public. But according to Scott, that law restricts some companies from doing business here.
“The 2014 amendment is so narrowly written that only Tesla Motors meets the requirements to sell in Pennsylvania,” said Scott. “But the EV landscape has changed significantly in the last 12 years, and more American EV manufacturers have brought products to market. If we don’t update the law, those manufacturers can’t sell here, simply because they don’t use the traditional car dealership model.”
Newer EV manufacturers include Lucid, Rivian and Scout. Scott’s bill would update the law so that all EV manufacturers have the same opportunities in the commonwealth. And, according to Scott, the bill would not make any changes to the state’s traditional franchise dealership system.
“Existing protections for local dealerships would remain fully intact,” said Scott. “This bill’s straightforward goal is to encourage competition and expand consumer choice in the EV marketplace, while attracting private investment, creating jobs and keeping business and tax revenue here in Pennsylvania.”
House Bill 2013 now goes to the full chamber for consideration. The bill is supported by all four EV manufacturers, including Tesla.

“Still, among the leading causes of death for firefighters is not just fire-related injury, but cancer. Cancer we now know is caused by repeated exposure to cancer-causing chemicals, like PFAS, found in firefighting foams and protective gear.
“Today’s committee approval of Representative Ciresi’s legislation to ensure all firefighters have access to annual cancer screenings is an important step in protecting our firefighting community and their families. I applaud the committee’s recognition of this often-invisible occupational hazard and their dedication to our volunteer and professional firefighters statewide.”
"Cancer is a devastating diagnosis. But if caught early and treatment can start, outcomes can be greatly improved,”
said Rep. Lisa Borowski,
co-chair of the caucus.
“Our first responders put their lives on the line every time they respond to a neighbor in need. It is time for us to respond to them and their health needs. House Bill 2394 will provide the resources they need to get potentially life-saving cancer screenings without incurring additional cost. This is a small way our grateful commonwealth can say 'thank you.'"
The bill would create a statewide program to ensure firefighters – both volunteer and professional – can receive annual cancer screenings at no cost, even when those services are not covered by their health insurance.

House Committee advances bill classifying medetomidine a Schedule III drug
Rep. Greg Scott
June 9, 2026 | 3:37 PM
HARRISBURG, June 9 –
State Reps. Greg Scott and Liz Hanbidge, both D-Montgomery, today announced the Pa. House Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee advanced their bill (H.B. 2529) that would classify the veterinary medicine medetomidine as a Schedule III controlled substance.
Medetomidine is a non-opioid sedative used by veterinarians. It is not approved for use in people. But data now shows that up to 80 percent of fentanyl samples tested in Pennsylvania contain it, increasing the risk of overdose for people who illegally use fentanyl.
“Today’s vote is an important first step in getting control of medetomidine’s use in the illegal drug market,” said Scott. “Too many lives are lost to opioids as it is. We don’t need these animal sedatives added to the mix and making it harder to reverse overdoses.”
According to Scott, a concern with medetomidine is that its sedative effects do not wear off if the overdose-reversing drug naloxone is used – though the lawmakers caution that in any suspected opioid overdose, naloxone should still be administered.
In 2024, Pennsylvania designated another sedative drug, xylazine, a Schedule III controlled substance. In response, the use of xylazine in street drugs declined. The representatives hope repeating this tactic with medetomidine will have the same impact.
“The growing presence of medetomidine in the illicit drug supply poses a serious threat to Pennsylvanians. Advancing this legislation out of committee is an important step toward confronting that danger and protecting lives,” said Hanbidge. “I am proud to co-sponsor this commonsense measure and look forward to its continued progress through the House and ultimately the Senate.”
“Between 75% and 90% of people experiencing withdrawal from medetomidine require ICU-level medical care,” said Scott. “This is a dangerous drug that presents extremely challenging situations for the first responders who need to administer overdose care. Everyone should be championing this bill.”
Classifying medetomidine as a Schedule III drug would still allow veterinarians to legally use the medicine for treating animals. The classification would require stricter storage by veterinary facilities.
This bill is a companion to
S.B. 866.

Pa. House votes to ban PFAS in cosmetics, dental floss, menstrual and baby products
Rep. Greg Scott
June 8, 2026 | 3:58 PM
HARRISBURG, June 8 —
State Rep. Greg Scott, D-Montgomery, today announced that the PA House passed his bill that would ban toxic PFAS forever chemicals from high-contact consumer products in Pennsylvania.
PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are synthetic chemicals linked to a range of serious health risks, including cancer, immune-system suppression, pregnancy-related hypertension, reduced fertility, and more. House Bill 2145 would ban the use of PFAS in the manufacture of many daily-use household products, including cosmetics, dental floss, infant and children’s products, and menstrual pads and tampons.
According to Scott, the focus on cosmetics, dental floss, menstrual products and many products used to care for children and babies is due to their daily, high-contact use.
“Pennsylvania’s legislature has been taking steps to reduce PFAS exposure in a variety of situations, and I’m proud to see my bill pass the House in our latest step to protect our residents from these harmful chemicals,” said Scott. “If we continue to allow toxic substances to be used in products that are intended for our most sensitive skin areas, or in products used daily by babies -- we’re not protecting Pennsylvanians. Over a lifetime of use, that’s too significant a risk of health complications.
“This bill targets a specific group of consumer products that industry experts tell us have a high rate of PFAS exposure,” said Scott. “My hope is that it serves as a starting point for future legislation to lower PFAS exposure even more in the Commonwealth.”
House Bill 2145 now heads to the state Senate for consideration.
Earlier this legislative session, the House also passed H.B. 1261 to ban the use of PFAS-containing firefighting foams and require the makers of firefighting gear to clearly label when that gear contains added PFAS chemicals. Scott helped author this legislation.

Rep. Scott Calls for comprehensive youth violence prevention strategy following tragic Norristown shooting
Rep. Greg Scott
June 4, 2026 | 3:37 PM
NORRISTOWN, June 4 --
Following the tragic shooting that claimed the life of a 15-year-old Norristown resident and the subsequent lockdown at Norristown Area High School, state Rep. Greg Scott issued the following statement:
"Norristown, enough is enough. What happened last night was a horrific tragedy.
“A young person is dead. Another young person now faces serious criminal charges. Families are grieving, students are hurting, and an entire community has been shaken. Whatever the circumstances, an incident like this traumatizes our community and impacts all of Norristown.
“Today's lockdown at Norristown Area High School only deepened the fear, anxiety, and uncertainty being experienced by students, parents, educators, and residents across our community. No child should have to learn in fear. No family should have to wonder whether their loved one will make it home safely.
“The young people of Norristown deserve leaders who are urgently focused on developing and implementing real solutions. Far too many young lives have been lost, and we cannot allow this level of violence to become accepted as normal.
“I am calling on
Norristown Municipal Council
and the
Norristown Police Department
to convene a community stakeholder meeting and immediately begin developing a comprehensive youth violence prevention strategy. Addressing this crisis requires intentional collaboration, strategic partnerships, and a shared commitment to action. I will be reaching out personally to council and police leaders to facilitate these discussions and get the work started -- we can't wait any longer.
“Leaders at every level of government, alongside clergy, educators, community organizations, families, and residents, must come together to create a coordinated plan that provides meaningful support, resources, opportunities, and intervention for young people before violence occurs.
“Nothing stops a bullet better than a job. We must invest in workforce development, mentorship, educational opportunities, recreation, mental health resources, violence intervention programs, and pathways that help young people see a future worth striving for. These are the investments I fight for in Harrisburg, and I want to be sure my work there is informed by all our local voices.
“Our goal must be to build a coordinated system of care that addresses the immediate needs of our youth while helping them recognize their potential, envision a brighter future, and believe in the possibilities that exist for their lives.
“There is no single solution to youth violence, but there is one thing we know for certain: Doing nothing is not an option. The time for conversations without action has passed. Our community deserves urgency. Our families deserve safety. And our young people deserve every opportunity to succeed.
“We owe them nothing less."
A copy of the Letter to Norristown Municipal Council can be found here.

Shusterman, Guzman and Scott to participate in AI safety hearing
State House will hold a public hearing on mitigating risks from frontier AI models
Rep. Greg Scott
October 13, 2026 | 12:23 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 13 –
State Reps. Melissa Shusterman, D-Chester, Manuel Guzman, D-Berks, and Gregg Scott, D-Montgomery, announced that their legislation,
HB 2800
and
HB 2829
, will be featured in the House Communications & Technology Committee’s public hearing on Mitigating Risks from Frontier AI Models at 10 a.m. Monday, Oct. 19 in room 205 Ryan Office Building in the Capitol Complex.
Frontier AI models are the most advanced artificial intelligence systems available and represent the leading-edge of AI technology and capabilities. These AI systems have been highlighted in news around the world in recent months for their alarming incidents and rogue behaviors which have caused
AI industry executives to call
for safety regulations and a slower pace of development.
A
recent Quinnipiac national poll
found that 86% of respondents support independent safety standards for AI companies, and that 73% are concerned about AI’s potential threat to human survival. Due to lack of action at the federal level to create safety measures, states have begun stepping up in recent months by passing several bills into law to address frontier AI models.
Shusterman, Guzman and Scott recently introduced legislation as they seek to fill this urgent need. The state House Communications & Technology Committee’s
public hearing
will include AI experts testifying on the emerging concerns surrounding frontier AI models, as well as the safety guardrails proposed by HBs 2800 and 2829.
“AI has the potential for technological advancements and benefits,” Shusterman said. “However, government must ensure frontier models are not causing catastrophic harm to society. This is my bare minimum expectation. Every other industry has governmental safeguards for good reasons – AI requires the same level, or more. The possibility of rogue AI agents is not acceptable to me, and I urge my fellow legislators of our Commonwealth, as well as officials at every level of government, to take these risks seriously and act quickly. Our citizens are counting on us.”
“I look forward to joining my colleagues and experts in AI research and safety for this important discussion on the risks posed by frontier AI models,” Guzman said. “We need clear safety standards, robust accountability frameworks, and greater transparency to ensure developers identify, assess, and address potential risks before deploying their systems. Innovation and public safety must go hand in hand.”
“AI may very well be the most powerful technological development some of us see in our lifetimes,” said Scott. “It has the potential to reshape everything we know about industry, technology, and society. We need to ensure that as these developments unfold, we’re providing the oversight necessary to make sure that reshaping is positive, that we understand the risks, and that there’s a framework in place to advance safely.”
